title: How Often Do You Really Need a Dental Cleaning?
meta_title: How Often Do You Really Need a Dental Cleaning? | Alexandria, VA
meta_description: Six months is a familiar guideline, not a universal rule. Your best cleaning schedule depends on gum health, cavity risk, age, home care and medical history.
h1: How often do adults and children really need dental cleanings?
intro: Twice a year is a useful starting point, but the best preventive schedule is based on the individual, not the calendar.
summary: Six months is a familiar guideline, not a universal rule. Your best schedule depends on gum health, cavity risk, age, home care and medical history.

sections.heading: Where six months came from
body: Most of us grew up hearing that everyone should have a cleaning every six months. It is a sensible default for a lot of adults and children, and insurance plans built their coverage around it. It was never meant as a prescription for every mouth.

Some people benefit from visits more often than twice a year. Others with consistently low risk can reasonably stretch the interval. What decides it is your gums, your cavity history, your home care, your age, your medical history and what we actually find at the visit.

sections.heading: Why professional cleanings still matter
body: Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and cleaning between the teeth are the foundation. Professional care does a different job. The hygienist removes plaque that has hardened into tartar, which no brush can shift, from above and just below the gum line, along with surface stain. The visit is also the moment someone measures your gums, looks at every tooth and filling, screens for oral cancer and adjusts your technique on your own teeth.

A cleaning, an exam and X-rays are related but not identical, and they do not have to be on identical schedules. Imaging is chosen by age, history, symptoms, findings and risk, not by the number of months that have passed. More on that on our [digital X-rays](/general-dentistry/digital-x-rays/) page.

sections.heading: Adults who often do better with more frequent visits
sections.intro: For many adults with healthy gums and average cavity risk, six months is appropriate. The interval shortens when risk rises, for example with:
items: A history of gum disease, which usually means periodontal maintenance every three to four months rather than a routine cleaning.
Persistent bleeding, inflammation or heavy tartar build-up.
Dry mouth, from medications or a medical condition.
Tobacco or nicotine use, including vaping.
Certain medical conditions or medications that affect oral health, such as diabetes.
Braces, aligners or dental work that is difficult to clean around.
Physical or cognitive limitations that make home care harder.

sections.heading: Periodontal maintenance is not a regular cleaning
body: Patients who have been treated for gum disease need a different visit: cleaning inside the pockets below the gum line, with full measurements compared against the last time. It is usually scheduled every three to four months, because the bacteria that cause gum disease re-establish on roughly that timeline. The interval depends on how the gums responded to treatment and on ongoing risk. Our [periodontal maintenance](/general-dentistry/periodontal-maintenance/) page explains the difference and why it matters.

sections.heading: How often should children have their teeth cleaned?
body: For many children, examinations and preventive visits are planned about every six months, starting by the first birthday. The interval should still reflect each child's needs. More frequent visits make sense when there are active cavities, a high risk of new decay, enamel concerns, orthodontic appliances, inconsistent home care or other findings. Recommendations also change as new teeth erupt and habits evolve.

A child's appointment is about more than removing plaque. It is where we watch growth, reinforce age-appropriate home care, apply fluoride and sealants when they are due, assess cavity risk and help a child become comfortable in a dental setting. See [children's dentistry](/general-dentistry/childrens-dentistry/).

sections.heading: Your schedule can change, in both directions
body: Risk is not permanent. Someone with decades of easy check-ups can develop dry mouth after starting a new medication and suddenly need fluoride and three-month visits. A teenager begins orthodontic treatment. Pregnancy, diet, dexterity, stress and changes in home care all shift the picture.

The reverse is true too. Better brushing, consistent cleaning between the teeth and control of existing disease can lengthen the interval again. The useful question is not whether everyone needs a cleaning every six months. It is what interval makes sense for you right now, and that is something we set together at each visit.

sections.heading: What to do between visits
items: Brush twice a day for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste, and spit rather than rinse.
Clean between the teeth daily with floss, interdental brushes or a water flosser.
Keep sugary and acidic foods and drinks to mealtimes.
Drink water regularly, especially if your mouth is dry.
Notice bleeding, sensitivity, pain or swelling, and mention it.
Wear a mouthguard for contact sports and a night guard if you grind.

sections.heading: Do not wait for the next planned cleaning
body: Pain, swelling, a broken tooth or persistent bleeding deserve a call sooner, whatever the calendar says. For busy households in West Alexandria, Seminary Hill, Fairlington and Shirlington, the realistic preventive plan is the one that fits both the clinical need and the family's ability to keep it, which is why we offer appointments from 7 AM on weekdays, into the evening, and on weekend mornings.

sections.heading: A note about online dental information
sections.body: This article is educational and cannot diagnose a condition or replace an examination. Recommendations depend on your symptoms, health history and clinical findings. Further reading: the American Dental Association on home oral care, and the American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry's periodicity recommendations.

faqs.q: Does everyone need exactly two cleanings a year?
faqs.a: No. Six months is a common and reasonable default, but the appropriate interval depends on individual risk and clinical findings. Some people need visits every three to four months; a few low-risk adults can stretch beyond six.

faqs.q: Is periodontal maintenance the same as a regular cleaning?
faqs.a: No. Periodontal maintenance is for patients who have been treated for gum disease. It cleans below the gum line inside the pockets, includes full measurements, and is usually scheduled more often. Insurance also treats it as a different procedure.

faqs.q: Should children follow the same schedule as adults?
faqs.a: Many children are seen about every six months, but the interval and the preventive services, such as fluoride and sealants, are individualized to the child's cavity risk and development.

cta.heading: Not sure when your next cleaning should be?
cta.body: Book an examination. We evaluate your teeth and gums, review your history, and recommend a preventive schedule tailored to you or your child.
